title: The Woman at the Well
lead: Jesus starts a conversation with someone others pass over, and she at once becomes an effective evangelist.
questions: Whom do you avoid so carefully that you take the long way around, and what would happen if next time you went straight ahead?
How do you begin your contact with people on the outside: with a request and with listening, or with a ready-made lecture?
Which part of your past, the part everyone has seen, could become your strongest testimony?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: John writes that Jesus “had to pass through Samaria.” It was the shortest route, and Josephus writes that Galileans went that way when they traveled to Jerusalem for the festivals. Relations between the two communities were tense, but the journey through Samaria was nothing unusual in itself. What is exceptional is what Jesus did at the well. At high noon God in the flesh sits down, “weary from His journey,” and says to the woman who comes up: “Give Me a drink.” Water was often drawn in the morning or the evening, and in company. The very fact that the woman came at noon and alone may be significant, but John says nothing about it. Jesus’ request meant more than we hear: in many eyes, a Samaritan woman’s jar was permanently unclean. Jesus doesn’t begin by giving, but by asking. The first gift to someone despised is the dignity of having something to offer.

The conversation about water becomes a conversation about thirst. “Living water” meant spring water, flowing on its own, as opposed to water standing in a cistern; Jesus promises a spring inside a person, not a tank to be refilled every day. The text does not say why she had had five husbands, or how much of those stories was her own choice. Jesus brings the truth about her life into the open without adding motives, and offers her living water. When the woman escapes into the dispute over the holy mountain, He neither flatters the Samaritan nor settles the argument in favor of His own side: God doesn’t live on any of our mountains, and “the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth.” And it is to her, a foreign woman with a difficult life story, that He answers the messianic hope with great clarity: “I who speak to you am He.”

The woman leaves her water jar and runs into town, and she turns her shame into an argument: “He told me everything I ever did.” If He knows everything and didn’t walk away, maybe He really is the One we’ve been waiting for. People come and listen to Jesus for two days, and in the end the Samaritans say what every evangelist longs to hear: we now believe not only because of your words; we have heard for ourselves. The map of the places we avoid is a map of how unlike Jesus we are. People who are looked down on don’t need a lecture. They need someone who will sit down by their well.

John writes that on His way from Judea to Galilee, Jesus “had to pass through Samaria.” That was the shortest route, and Josephus writes that Galileans usually traveled this way to Jerusalem for the festivals. Samaria could be avoided, however, because relations between the two communities were often tense. So the “had to” on its own does not prove that Jesus was breaking a universal ban on travel. This story leaves the beaten track only at the well. In Samaria, a person was waiting for Him. This part of the series speaks of God coming to the avoided, and no one in the Gospels is ignored as systematically as the Samaritans: an entire people you don’t visit, plus one woman whom even her own people pushed to the margins.

sections.heading: A Well at High Noon
paragraphs: It all happens near the town of Sychar, in the field Jacob gave to Joseph, by a well bearing the patriarch’s name, still standing today beside the main north–south road. John includes a detail you couldn’t invent at a desk. Once he calls the place a dug well, and once a spring. That sounds inconsistent, until you stand over the well itself, which is both at once: a deep shaft cut into the rock, and living water welling up from its bottom. There Jesus sits down, “weary from His journey,” about the sixth hour, which is to say at high noon. Here the incarnation has its simplest illustration: God, worn out from walking, sits on the rim of a well and wants a drink, and a woman with a water jar appears beside Him. Water was often drawn in the morning or the evening, in the cool of the day. The very fact that the woman came at noon, and alone, may be significant, but John does not say that her neighbors had rejected her, or why she chose that hour. So facing each other at the well sit a Jew and a Samaritan, a man and a woman, a Teacher and a person the town talked about in whispers. Each of those pairs is a separate wall.

sections.heading: Give Me a Drink
paragraphs: Jesus starts the conversation with a request. Just as in yesterday’s story: before He gives anything, He first asks. “Give Me a drink” meant more than we hear. In the eyes of many teachers of that time, Samaritan vessels were permanently unclean. Later rabbis would put it bluntly, teaching that the daughters of the Samaritans are unclean from the cradle. To ask a Samaritan woman for water from her jar was to accept defilement. So the woman’s astonishment is entirely in place: “You are a Jew… How can You ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” There were pious men who closed their eyes when they passed a woman in the street. Jesus closed His eyes to no one. There is something more in His request: He doesn’t begin by giving. He begins by making her needed. The first gift to a despised person is not charity but the dignity of being someone who has something to offer.

sections.heading: Living Water
paragraphs: From here the conversation becomes a game played on two levels. Jesus speaks of “living water,” which was the ordinary name for running water, spring water, as opposed to the standing water of cisterns. The woman hears plumbing: “You have nothing to draw with and the well is deep.” Yet for centuries a deeper current had flowed through that expression: the river flowing out of Eden, the spring coming from under the threshold of the temple in the prophet’s vision, God’s lament that His people had forsaken “the fountain of living water” and dug for themselves “broken cisterns.” Israel’s ritual piety knew the difference in its everyday practice. In the mikveh, a ritual washing was valid only in living water, and when there wasn’t enough, some was kept in a separate pool to make hand-drawn water fit for use. So Jesus is telling the woman at the well: what you’re looking for, drawing it from the shaft every day, exists in a form that flows on its own. “The water I give him will become in him a fount of water springing up to eternal life.” Not a tank to be filled, but a spring of your own, inside. Then, with a single sentence, He touches the place where her life is leaking: “You have had five husbands, and the man you now have is not your husband.” He does not say this to humiliate her. We do not know why her life had turned out this way, or how much of those stories was her own choice. Jesus brings the truth of her life story into the open without adding motives, and the conversation about water becomes a conversation about thirst.

sections.heading: A Wound, Not a Debate
paragraphs: The woman does what all of us do when a conversation becomes uncomfortable: she changes the subject to a religious dispute. “Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you Jews say that the place where one must worship is in Jerusalem.” It’s easy to miss, but she isn’t pointing at a temple. She is pointing at an empty mountain. The sanctuary on Gerizim, a real building with priests and walls, had been destroyed a hundred and fifty years earlier by a Jewish ruler, the same one who leveled Shechem. The woman is defending an empty place before a descendant of those who destroyed it. This dispute was not academic. Each side had its own version of the Five Books of Moses, differing even in the wording of the commandments, and they shared the same fathers, whose inheritance was the object of a quiet war, including around this very well. Jesus’ answer is astonishing from two sides at once. He doesn’t flatter her: “Salvation is from the Jews,” He says firmly; truth is not up for social negotiation. Nor does He take His own people’s side: “A time is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.” True worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth. God doesn’t live on any of our mountains. The Father is seeking worshipers, not places. Where two communities have been tallying their arguments for centuries, Jesus moves the question from “where” to “how” and “Whom.”

sections.heading: I Am He
paragraphs: Then the woman speaks of her hope: “I know that Messiah… is coming.” And Jesus answers with words spoken for the first time in this Gospel: “I who speak to you am He.” We need to grasp the scale of that admission. This is one of the clearest places in the Gospels where Jesus answers directly the messianic hope of the person He is talking to. In Judea and Galilee the word “Messiah” was so charged with politics and armies that it couldn’t be spoken without the risk of an uprising. Even in Samaria, messianic hope could stir people up to fight: a few years later an armed crowd would go up Gerizim behind a man who promised to show them the sacred vessels hidden by Moses, and Pilate would crush them with his cavalry and lose his office because of it. What’s more, the woman was waiting for someone a little different from the Messiah the Jews expected: her people looked not for a king from David’s line but for a prophet like Moses, who would explain everything. Jesus doesn’t correct her ideas about the Messiah, nor does He make her first adopt Jerusalem’s expectations. He answers the hope she actually has. So the first full “It is I” in this Gospel was spoken not before scholars or crowds, but at a well, to a foreign woman with a torn-up life story, in a country you don’t visit. God often says the most important things to the people we look down on.

sections.heading: The Abandoned Water Jar
paragraphs: The woman leaves her water jar and runs into town. That abandoned vessel is a whole commentary: she came for water and leaves with the spring; she can come back for the jar later. In town she says something perfect from a psychological point of view: “Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did. Could this be the Christ?” A woman whose past everyone knew turns it into an argument. What had been her shame becomes her testimony: if He knows everything and didn’t walk away, maybe He really is the One we’ve been waiting for. The town follows her. The Samaritans ask Him to stay, and Jesus spends two days among people with whom a Jew doesn’t spend the night. At the end comes a sentence every evangelist would love to hear: “We now believe not only because of your words; we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this man truly is the Savior of the world.” Her testimony brought them to the threshold; from there they went on by themselves. And the seed sown at this well would keep growing long after the sower had gone. When, years later, Philip the deacon comes to Samaria with the gospel, he will be reaping a harvest from a field Someone else had sown at high noon beside Jacob’s well. Jesus told His disciples so that very day: “One sows and another reaps.”

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: This story begins with a route. First: the most devout went around; Jesus went straight through, because along the way through the avoided territory there was a person. Every community, ours included, has its Samaria: people and circles you don’t visit, the ones everyone knows in advance are “not our kind.” The map of the places we avoid is a map of how unlike Jesus we are. Second: Jesus talked before He taught. He asked for water, listened, answered her questions, and didn’t preach a single sermon. People who get avoided don’t need a lecture first, only someone who will sit down by their well and ask for something only they can give. And third: the most effective evangelist in this Gospel turned out to be a woman with a life story no committee would ever have approved for a witness. God doesn’t wait to send a person until their past is fit for a display case. Sometimes it is precisely the life story everyone stared at that makes the testimony impossible to refute: He told me everything I ever did, and He didn’t walk away.
